newsitem.title: ZAIRE: "Non-armed" opposition demands role in Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: "Non-armed" opposition demands role in Zaire talks.

text.p: Zaire's radical opposition, which commands a fanatical following in Kinshasa's teeming shantytowns, on Thursday demanded a seat at any negotiations between President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila on ending civil war.
Statements by senior opposition figures were the clearest sign of a looming power struggle between Kabila and opposition chieftain Etienne Tshisekedi.
One close Tshisekedi associate even predicted Zaire would be ungovernable if rebels gained power and excluded the civil opposition from power.
The civil opposition has been flexing its muscles since Kabila's forces turned their sights on Kinshasa after seizing half of the country in a six-month-old war to topple Mobutu.
In Cape Town, the U.N.'s special envoy on Zaire said Mobutu and Kabila had agreed in principle to meet for talks.
"The outcome we have today (is) the agreement in principle by the two parties to meet at the highest level... to discuss transitional arrangements," U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun told a news conference.
In Kinshasa, powerful opposition member of parliament Andre Boboliko told Reuters Tshisekedi's camp was entitled to join the talks because of its long campaign for democracy.
"There is an armed opposition, a non-armed opposition and those in power. Real negotiations have to include all three forces," said Boboliko, a deputy speaker of parliament.
Boboliko, who masterminded last month's ousting of prime minister Kengo wa Dondo by parliament, was echoed by another radical opposition lawmaker, Joseph Olenghankoy.
"The rebels must understand that there is a democratic opposition which has always battled inside the country," Olenghankoy told BBC Africa Service radio.

"If one believes that a solution is Kabila-Mobutu, even if Kabila comes to take over the (capital) town after Mobutu and installs himself in power, I assure you that this country will never be governable," he added.
Kabila headed back to Zaire on Thursday after talks in South Africa with President Nelson Mandela, whose country is mediating in the Zaire conflict.

While rebels advance on Kinshasa, Mobutu's government is facing mounting pressure from the pro-Tshisekedi opposition, which brought Kinshasa to a standstill on Monday and Tuesday with anti-Mobutu protests.

Political analysts say Monday's stay-at-home protest and other measures planned by the opposition are intended to demonstrate to Kabila that Tshisekedi is a force to be reckoned with in future power sharing.
"There has to be a tripartite meeting where there will be Mobutu, Tshisekedi and Kabila," Olenghankoy said.
Political analysts have predicted a power tussle or even outright confrontation between Kabila and the Tshisekedi camp once their common enemy, Mobutu, is no longer an issue.

At the root of such fears is the very nature of Kabila's rebellion. The civil war started when ethnic-Tutsis or Banyamulenge in eastern Zaire took up arms after authorities threatened to expel them to the ancestral homeland in Rwanda.
Although the rebel force has expanded to include other ethnic groups, military analysts say Kabila's shock troops, key to the rebels' whirlwind advances, are largely Tutsi.

Zaire insists that Kabila is fighting a proxy war for neighbouring Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi. Tutsis dominate the armies of Rwanda and Burundi and Uganda has historic links to the leadership in Rwanda. All three states deny involvement.
The backbone of the radical opposition is Tshisekedi's Baluba tribespeople, the largest ethnic group in Zaire and the majority group in the capital's five million population.

"Right now the radical opposition is happy Kabila is doing what they have failed to achieve for years, that is removing Mobutu from power. Their attitude is that they will deal with their differences with Kabila later," one analyst said.
